newsitem.title: USA: Oil prices hit new post-Gulf War highs.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices hit new post-Gulf War highs.

text.p: Crude oil prices hit a post-Gulf War high Wednesday as worries about low heating oil stocks outweighed weather forecasts that a cold front headed for New England would be milder than expected.
Weather concerns also pushed coffee and wheat prices higher as traders worried about a looming cold front in Mexico, torrential rains in Argentina and a possible "winter kill" of U.S. winter wheat.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude for January delivery settled up 45 cents at $26.16 a barrel and rose as high as $26.20 in late trading, eclipsing the old post-Gulf War high of $26.10 recorded Oct. 22.

"There is zero tolerance for error in the supply-demand balance," said Bob MacMinn, president of petroleum consulting firm MPAS in Toronto. "Heating oil inventories are low, but demand has been high and it's not even winter yet."
January heating oil finished up 0.64 cent a gallon at 74.18 cents, while January gasoline settled up 1.40 cents at 71.17 cents a gallon after setting a contract high of 71.50.
Heating oil had fallen as low as 72.20 cents after cold weather expected in the Northeast was forecast to be not as drastic as first thought and a rise in stockpiles was reported.
The Midwest was hit with heavy snowstorms and bitter cold earlier this week, and many predicted arctic air was headed for the Northeast, the world's largest heating oil market.

But Weather Services Corp. said Wednesday that the cold would moderate in the Northeast, where temperatures will be 8 degrees below normal by Saturday, and the National Weather Service's six-to-10-day predicted normal temperatures in most of the region.
Heating oil supplies are growing but are still well below those of a year ago.
Traders also shrugged off the first Iraqi oil shipments under a United Nations deal allowing limited sales so Iraq can buy food, medicine and other humanitarian goods.
Fourteen countries already have confirmed signing contracts with Iraq for almost 400,000 barrels a day.

"We do not expect Iraq's return to have a significant downward impact on oil prices in the very short term since the market is likely to absorb the country's additional exports during the winter months," finance house Kleinwort Benson said in a report.
Cold weather also played a role in the coffee market, where concerns that the cold front approaching central Mexico could pose a threat to that country's coffee crop boosted prices.
March coffee futures at the New York Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange closed 2 cents per pound higher at 111.90 cents as speculators bought contracts.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, March wheat closed 6-1/2 cents a bushel higher at $4.00-3/4 on concerns about the extent of losses to Argentina's wheat crop from torrential rains and possible "winter kill" damage in U.S. winter wheat fields.
"It was up on uncertainty in Argentina, fund buying and the cold weather," said Ron Kucha of O'Connor and Co.
